title: Find the Number of K-Even Arrays
statement:
Consider arrays `arr` of length `n` in which every entry is an integer from `1` to `m`, inclusive. An index `i` with `0 <= i < n - 1` is *marked* when the number `arr[i] * arr[i + 1] - arr[i] - arr[i + 1]` is even, and an array is called **k-even** when exactly `k` of its indices are marked.

Return how many different k-even arrays of length `n` there are. The count can be huge, so return it modulo `10^9 + 7`.
signature: int countOfArrays(int n, int m, int k)
notes:
## Intuition

Rewrite the test: `a·b − a − b = (a − 1)(b − 1) − 1`, which is even exactly when `(a − 1)(b − 1)` is odd, that is, when **both** `a` and `b` are even. So an index is marked when two even values are neighbours, and only the even/odd pattern matters: each even position has `evens = ⌊m / 2⌋` choices and each odd one `odds = m − evens`. Rather than trying all `m^n` arrays, build them left to right, remembering only the number of marks so far and the parity of the last value.

## Approach

1. Count `evens` and `odds` among `1..m`.
2. `endEven[marked]` and `endOdd[marked]` count the arrays of the current `length` with exactly `marked` marks whose last value is even or odd. Length 1 has no marks: `endEven[0] = evens`, `endOdd[0] = odds`.
3. For each next `length`, an appended odd value never adds a mark: `nextOdd[marked] = (endEven[marked] + endOdd[marked]) · odds`.
4. An appended even value adds a mark only after an even value: `nextEven[marked] = (fromOdd + fromEven) · evens`, where `fromOdd = endOdd[marked]` and `fromEven = endEven[marked − 1]`.
5. Reduce modulo `10^9 + 7` throughout. After length `n`, return `endEven[k] + endOdd[k]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`n = 3`, `m = 4`, `k = 2`, so `evens = 2` (2 and 4) and `odds = 2`.

- Length 1: `endEven = [2, 0, 0]`, `endOdd = [2, 0, 0]`.
- Length 2: `nextOdd = [8, 0, 0]` and `nextEven = [2·2, 2·2, 0] = [4, 4, 0]`.
- Length 3: `nextEven[2] = (endOdd[2] + endEven[1]) · 2 = 8` and `nextOdd[2] = 0`.

The answer is `8 + 0 = 8`: every value must be even.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n · k): each of the `n − 1` steps fills `k + 1` entries.
- Space: O(k) for the rolling arrays.

## Pitfalls

- The test is not "the product is even": for `2` and `3`, `6 − 2 − 3 = 1` is odd, so that index is not marked.
- With `m = 1` there is no even value: the answer is 1 when `k = 0` and 0 otherwise.
- Build fresh `nextEven` and `nextOdd` arrays; updating in place mixes two lengths.
- Reduce every step so that `count · evens` stays far below 2^53.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MOD` | the modulus `10^9 + 7` |
| `evens`, `odds` | how many values in `1..m` are even, odd |
| `endEven`, `endOdd` | counts for the current length by number of marks, ending even or odd |
| `nextEven`, `nextOdd` | the same counts one position longer |
| `length` | the length being built |
| `marked` | number of marked indices |
| `fromOdd`, `fromEven` | arrays an even value can extend to reach `marked` marks |

narration.3: Only parity matters for the test, so count the even values in 1..m...
narration.5: endEven[marked] counts arrays of the current length with that many marks whose last value is even.
narration.6: endOdd[marked] does the same for arrays that end in an odd value.
narration.7: A single even value: no neighbours yet, so no marks.
narration.8: A single odd value, also with no marks.
narration.10: Grow the arrays one position at a time.
narration.13: Fill in every possible number of marks up to k; more than k can never shrink back.
narration.14: An odd value never makes a marked pair, so the mark count stays the same whatever came before.
narration.15: An even value after an odd one adds no mark...
narration.16: ...but after an even one it marks the index between them, so it extends arrays with one mark fewer.
narration.17: Each of those arrays can be extended by any of the even values.
narration.19: The new length becomes the current one.
narration.22: Arrays of length n with exactly k marks end in either parity.
